implementation_notes: JavaScript's built-in Array has no heap, so this is a small library (a sorted-array insert is O(n) per push and a common mistake) or a heap implementation on top of an array. For moderate sizes (a few thousand), a sorted array with binary-search insert and pop-from-the-end is often faster than a binary heap in JavaScript because the V8 array operations are highly optimized and the heap's cache-unfriendly sift is not worth avoiding at that scale. For large sizes or frequent updates, use a heap library with a decrease-key / index-map API. In Node.js, a worker-priority queue should wrap access in a mutex because the JS event loop gives no protection against interleaving across await points. Note that typed arrays do not have a heap, and a Map iteration order is insertion order, not priority order.
idiom_name: sorted array with binary-search insert for small N; a heap library with an index map for large N or frequent updates
pitfalls: [].sort on every push or a linear scan for the minimum is O(n^2) overall and is the most common wrong implementation.
For a Dijkstra-style frontier, a library without decrease-key forces either re-push with stale-entry skipping or an O(n) removal scan.
The JS event loop does not protect a priority queue across await points - two concurrent handlers can interleave between a poll and a push.
An unbounded priority queue in an event-driven system is a memory leak: bound it and state the drop policy.
